performers: Musopen Symphony (Commons credit; ensemble attribution disputed)
intro: The violas are already moving when the violins begin their restless G minor tune. A falling semitone gets under the skin of the whole movement, returning in fragments and in a second theme that comes home changed.

relations.label: The opening returns in the recapitulation
relations.basis: The first-theme group returns in G minor after the development; the measured later span agrees with the recapitulation marked near 194 s. This performance omits the exposition repeat. CENS diagonal mean 0.972, sustained 22 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 193.5 s (cache/form/mozart-40-molto-allegro.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Already in motion
cues.text: The violas set a quiet, restless pulse. Over it the violins repeat notes and fall a semitone, then do it again. Mozart begins in mid-thought: no grand opening chord, just that small phrase unable to leave itself alone.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), I, opening bars. The violin theme and its development are discussed by Matthew Lorenzon, ABC Classic: https://www.abc.net.au/listen/classic/read-and-watch/music-reads/mozart-symphony-no-40-sonata-form/10160386.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Semitones in B♭ major
cues.text: Strings and woodwinds exchange the second theme in B♭ major. It has longer breaths than the opening, but small chromatic steps still run through the melody. The change of key brings warmth without quite bringing rest.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), I, second subject. Lorenzon’s ABC Classic account describes its chromatic semitones and relative-major key.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A room with a garden
cues.text: In June 1788 Mozart moves to cheaper lodgings outside central Vienna. Writing to Michael Puchberg, he welcomes fewer visitors, more time to work and a garden. A hired carriage can still take him into town when business calls.
cues.evidence: Mozart to Michael Puchberg, before 17 June 1788, Bauer–Deutsch 1077, pp. 1–2: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/raradocs/transcr/pdf_eng/1077_WAM_Puchberg_1788.pdf.

cues.title: An abrupt F♯ minor
cues.text: The development opens with the familiar violin tune in F♯ minor, far from the B♭ major close. Soon only its first few notes remain. Strings and winds pass those scraps among themselves, beginning new entries before the previous ones have finished.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), I, development. Lorenzon’s ABC Classic account describes the repeated opening cell; the score establishes the F♯ minor opening.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The violins recover G minor
cues.text: The opening tune returns over the moving viola accompaniment. Its route onward is longer now: Mozart expands the connecting passage and keeps working the little fragments between the first and second themes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), I, recapitulation. The expanded transition is documented by Matthew Lorenzon, ABC Classic.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The second tune comes home
cues.text: The second theme now belongs to G minor. Strings and winds still trade its small, winding phrases, but the changed notes take away the warmth of its first appearance. The two themes finally share a key.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), I, recapitulated second subject; Lorenzon’s ABC Classic account describes the home-key return.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Winds hold, strings answer
cues.text: Quiet wind chords hang above the answering strings near the close. The orchestra then returns to forceful chords and running notes for the last G minor cadences.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), I, final extension and cadence.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: F major, then a breath
transitions.to: B · Strings and winds in B♭
transitions.how: The transition gathers on F major, the dominant of B♭, and breaks off. Quiet strings and woodwinds begin the second theme in B♭ major after this pause. Their longer, chromatic phrases replace the preceding orchestral rush; the tempo stays Molto allegro.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), I, transition into the second subject. Matthew Lorenzon, ABC Classic, describes the change from the forceful orchestral bridge to the chromatic second theme.

transitions.title: B♭ major to F♯ minor
transitions.from: B · Strings and winds in B♭
transitions.to: Dev · The tune in F♯ minor
transitions.how: The exposition closes in B♭ major. Mozart immediately shifts to F♯ minor, where the violins recover the first theme over soft wind chords. Its repeated notes and falling semitone remain familiar in this remote key; the melody soon breaks into shorter, overlapping entries.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), I, end of exposition and opening of development.

transitions.title: Fragments settle over D
transitions.from: Dev · The tune in F♯ minor
transitions.to: A′ · G minor and the violin tune
transitions.how: The harmony settles on D, the dominant of G minor, while the remaining fragments grow quieter. The bassoon descends above a held horn D. The violins then recover their full opening phrase over the moving violas, back in G minor.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), I, final bars of the development and main-theme return.

transitions.title: The pause leads to G minor
transitions.from: A′ · G minor and the violin tune
transitions.to: B′ · The second theme turns minor
transitions.how: The expanded transition reaches D major, the dominant of G minor. Another break releases the second theme, now in G minor. Strings and woodwinds retain their quiet exchange, with B♭ supplying the minor third above G.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), I, recapitulatory transition and second subject. The changed key and enlarged transition are discussed by Matthew Lorenzon, ABC Classic.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
